label: Password spraying vs brute force vs credential stuffing

mentor.diagnosis: You called a low and slow attack brute force. The tell is the direction of the attempts and the lockout behaviour.
contrast: One account, huge failure count, locked out fast
One common password against many accounts
Many accounts, one or two failures each, no lockouts
Username and password pairs leaked from another breach
Successes mixed with failures, often from unusual locations
mentor.rule: Spraying is wide and shallow, deliberately staying under the lockout threshold. Brute force is narrow and deep.
mentor.tell: 'A single failed login against each of two hundred accounts, no accounts locked' is spraying.
mentor.trap: Account lockout stops brute force and does nothing against spraying, which is why spraying is used. Answering lockout to a spraying scenario is the paired error.

mentor.diagnosis: You called self propagating malware a virus. The exam separates them on exactly one point: whether it needs a user or a host file.
contrast: No, it is a standalone program
Yes, someone runs the infected file
As fast as users share files
Across the network on its own, often in minutes
Many hosts compromised quickly with no user involvement
mentor.rule: If it spread across the network with nobody clicking anything, it is a worm.
mentor.tell: 'Dozens of hosts infected within the hour with no reported user action' is a worm, and it is why containment by segmentation comes first.
mentor.trap: Virus is the everyday word for all malware, so it is the reflex answer. The exam uses it strictly.

mentor.diagnosis: You matched on the outcome rather than on the defining behaviour. Each of these names a different stage.
contrast: Pretends to be something the user wants
The user installed a useful looking tool
Hides itself, often below the OS
Tools show nothing wrong but the behaviour persists, or it survives a reinstall
The attacker keeps returning after the password was reset
Waits for a condition, then fires
Triggered on a date, or after an employee was removed from payroll
mentor.rule: Trojan is how it arrived. Rootkit is how it hides. Backdoor is how the attacker returns. Logic bomb is when it fires.
mentor.tell: 'Antivirus reports the system as clean but the behaviour continues' is a rootkit. The only reliable remedy is to reimage.
mentor.trap: A rootkit usually arrives as a trojan and installs a backdoor, so all three are present in the story. Answer the part the question actually asks about.

label: Spyware vs bloatware, and when unwanted software is actually malicious

mentor.diagnosis: You judged by how annoying the software is rather than by what it does and whether it was meant to be there. Bloatware is unwanted; spyware is hostile. Only one of them is an attack.
contrast: Preinstalled by a vendor, or bundled with a wanted install
Installed covertly, often by a trojan or a drive-by
No, though it enlarges the attack surface
Remove it as part of hardening a build
Treat as an incident: investigate scope and persistence
mentor.rule: Bloatware wastes resources and adds unpatched software you never chose. Spyware exfiltrates. If the stem mentions data leaving, it is not bloatware.
mentor.tell: Preinstalled vendor utilities on a new fleet points to bloatware. Credentials appearing elsewhere points to spyware.
mentor.trap: Bloatware is a real security problem for an unglamorous reason: it is third-party software, running with privilege, that nobody is patching. Dismissing it as a performance complaint is the error.

label: Physical brute force, RFID cloning and environmental attacks

mentor.diagnosis: You looked for a network path. Several indicators in this objective are physical, and an attacker who can reach the building or its power does not need one.
contrast: Forces a door, cabinet or lock
Damage, forced entry, a device missing or added
Reads a badge at close range and reproduces it
One badge used in two places, or outside its holder's pattern
Attacks power, cooling or fire suppression
Thermal shutdown, a tripped supply, equipment failing together
Denies access to a resource by any means
Users cannot reach a service that is otherwise healthy
Exhausts a resource so it cannot serve
Saturated link, exhausted connections, filled storage
mentor.rule: An environmental attack targets the conditions equipment needs rather than the equipment. Disabling cooling in a server room takes the estate down without touching a single packet.
mentor.tell: A cloned badge seen in two buildings, a room running hot, or a failure affecting everything in one location at once.
mentor.trap: RFID cloning needs only proximity, often seconds in a lift or a queue. Treating badge possession as proof of identity is what makes it work, which is why badges pair with a second factor on sensitive doors.

label: Amplified vs reflected distributed denial of service

mentor.diagnosis: You used the two terms as if they were one. Most large attacks are both, and the exam still separates them.
contrast: Spoof the victim's address, send requests to third parties, replies land on the victim
Hides the source and uses innocent servers
Choose a protocol where a small request produces a large reply
Spoofed requests to open DNS or NTP resolvers
All UDP, since UDP does not verify the source
mentor.rule: Reflection is about who appears to send it. Amplification is about how much comes back. Spoofing the source makes reflection possible.
mentor.tell: 'A 60 byte query producing a 3,000 byte response' is amplification. 'Traffic arriving from thousands of legitimate DNS servers' is reflection.
mentor.trap: They almost always appear together in real attacks, so both options look correct. Read whether the question emphasises the size multiplier or the disguised origin.

label: On-path attack vs replay vs session hijacking

mentor.diagnosis: You matched on 'the attacker was in the middle' without checking whether they modified traffic live or resent it later.
contrast: Sits between the parties and can read or alter traffic in real time
Captures a valid message and sends it again later
Takes over an established session, usually with a stolen token
Secure and HttpOnly cookies, rebinding the session, short lifetimes
One time values, Kerberos timestamps, MFA
mentor.rule: On-path is live interception. Replay is a recording played back. A nonce or timestamp defeats replay and does nothing about on-path.
mentor.tell: 'The captured authentication request was submitted again an hour later and was accepted' is replay, and the fix is a nonce or timestamp.
mentor.trap: Replay usually requires an on-path position to capture the traffic in the first place, so both are present in the story. Answer the mechanism the question describes.

label: Reading indicators of compromise in authentication data

mentor.diagnosis: You read a single log line instead of the pattern. Each of these indicators names a specific shape in the data.
contrast: Successful logins from distant locations closer together than travel allows
Credential compromise, or a VPN in use
One account active in two places at once
Brute force, or a stale saved password
Activity at a time this account never works
A gap where events should be
mentor.rule: Missing logs are an indicator, not an absence of one. A gap is evidence that something removed it.
mentor.tell: 'Authenticated from London at 09:02 and from Singapore at 09:20' is impossible travel, and the first response is to verify with the user.
mentor.trap: Impossible travel has a high false positive rate from VPNs and cloud egress. It is still the correct name for the indicator.

label: Downgrade vs collision vs birthday attack

mentor.diagnosis: You grouped these as 'crypto attacks' without separating what each one actually targets.
contrast: Force both parties to agree on a weaker cipher or protocol version
Find two different inputs producing the same digest
Exploit probability so collisions are found far faster than brute force suggests
Downgrade: disable legacy versions, require minimum TLS
Collision: use SHA-256 or better, retire MD5 and SHA-1
mentor.rule: Downgrade attacks the negotiation, not the algorithm. Collision and birthday attack the hash, with birthday describing why collisions are cheaper than intuition suggests.
mentor.tell: 'The client and server were forced to negotiate SSL 3.0' is a downgrade. 'Two different documents produced the same MD5 digest' is a collision.
mentor.trap: A downgrade attack ends with weak cryptography being broken, so it looks like an algorithm weakness. The flaw is that the weak option was still offered.

label: Privilege escalation vs directory traversal vs forgery vs injection

mentor.diagnosis: You named an application attack by its outcome rather than by the mechanism the stem described.
contrast: A standard user ended up with administrative access
Escaping the intended path to read other files
Sequences such as ../../ in a file parameter
Making a victim's browser or server send a request the attacker chose
The action ran as the victim, who never intended it
Input interpreted as code by a downstream interpreter
SQL fragments, commands, LDAP filters in a parameter
Writing past the end of allocated memory
Oversized input, crash, then controlled execution
mentor.rule: Name the mechanism, not the consequence. Most of these can end in the attacker gaining control, so the outcome does not identify them.
mentor.tell: Path sequences in a parameter are traversal. A parameter interpreted by another system is injection. Extra rights obtained afterwards are escalation.
mentor.trap: Privilege escalation is the result of many different attacks, so it is always defensible and usually not the specific answer wanted.

label: Evil twin vs rogue access point

mentor.diagnosis: You used the two terms interchangeably. They overlap, but the exam separates them by intent and by whether the name is cloned.
contrast: Any unauthorised AP on the network
An AP impersonating a legitimate SSID
An employee plugging in their own AP
Get clients to associate so traffic can be captured or modified
Wireless IPS looking for duplicate SSIDs
mentor.rule: Every evil twin is a rogue AP. Not every rogue AP is an evil twin. The cloned SSID is the tell.
mentor.tell: 'Same SSID as corporate, stronger signal, users reconnected automatically' is an evil twin, usually leading to an on-path attack.
mentor.trap: Rogue AP is the broader and safer sounding term, so it attracts the answer. If the SSID was impersonated, evil twin is the more precise answer and the exam wants precision.
